There's a long-running joke that Apple always solemnly announces that each year's iPhone Pro is "the best iPhone we've ever made," as if that were somehow surprising. But I do feel a touch of melancholy about the iPhone 18 Pro, because if the rumors about next year's model are true, this could be the last generation of the form factor that began with 2017's iPhone X.

More specifically, we expect to see a major step toward the "single slab of glass" vision next year, bringing the incremental changes of the past decade to a close…

The Evolution of the iPhone Pro Lineup

If you line up every generation from the iPhone 12 Pro to the iPhone 16 Pro, I think most people would struggle to tell them apart, apart from 2022's switch from the notch to the Dynamic Island. The iPhone 17 Pro only stands out because of the elongated camera plateau and the cosmic orange color.

Of course, each generation brings new features, but I think it's true that unless a particular feature is personally useful to you, you really have to skip at least two or three generations to feel any meaningful upgrade.

This is absolutely not intended as a criticism of Apple. The reality is that the high-end smartphone is now a mature technology, at least in the traditional form factor. You simply won't see huge differences between consecutive generations, because there's only so much you can improve on a year-over-year basis.

Apple is now starting to experiment with different form factors, beginning with the iPhone Air, and now of course the iPhone Duo—and we expect another major design breakthrough next year, with that 20th anniversary model.

It's still a bit unclear how Apple will position next year's design. Early rumors suggested it would be a standalone model, separate from the iPhone 19 Pro lineup, but other reports suggest it will be next year's Pro model. There's also the question of whether Apple will stick with sequential numbering or skip a number to mark the milestone, so it could also be called the iPhone 20 Pro.

For my part, I do expect it will be the new iPhone Pro design, whether Apple calls it 19 or 20. If this assumption is correct, the iPhone 18 Pro will be the last generation of the form factor we've used for six years.

I'm jumping two full generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I'll list the additions from each year separately. I'll skip upgrades I consider trivial or totally irrelevant to me, like going from a 6-core GPU to a 7-core one and GenLock.

iPhone 17 Pro Features Carried Over

  • Center Stage front camera for photos and video calls
  • Super-stabilized video
  • Dual-capture simultaneous recording
  • Telephoto increased from 5x to 8x
  • Telephoto sensor increased from 12MP to 48MP
  • ProRes RAW video
  • Longer battery life
  • Faster charging

iPhone 18 Pro New Features

  • Larger maximum aperture on main camera
  • Variable aperture main camera
  • Pro camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)
  • Photographic Styles generation 3
  • Smart focus tracking
  • Cinematic mode effect added to standard video
  • Tap-to-zoom-and-rotate front camera
  • Smaller Dynamic Island capable of displaying three Live Activities
  • (Even) longer battery life
  • (Even) faster charging

My Personal ... Highlights

For me, there are five features I'll be focusing on during my initial use.

Variable aperture lens

Although the standout feature is the variable aperture lens, I've said before that we shouldn't expect too much. The maximum aperture is only slightly wider on such a small sensor, so I don't expect much difference in terms of shallow depth of field effects.

However, the wider maximum aperture does allow roughly two-thirds of a stop more light. Whether this makes a practical difference remains to be seen, but in theory it should allow for shorter exposure times in Night mode. Night mode is a feature I use frequently, and often handheld, so I'm quite looking forward to trying it out.

Pro camera controls

Having control over shutter speed will definitely be useful for shots like panning. Full control over white balance will also be very handy. I also expect the histogram to be very useful when manually setting exposure.

I'm generally not someone who likes using filters when shooting or editing on iPhone, preferring to make adjustments later in the traditional way. So I rarely use the existing Photographic Styles feature, and I don't expect to use the latest version much either. However, I must admit the film presets have piqued my interest a little, so I'll definitely give them a try.

One of the biggest weaknesses of autofocus when shooting video is that when the subject is briefly obscured by another object, the camera may shift focus to that obstruction. Smart focus tracking claims to solve this problem, so I'll definitely be testing it.

Cinematic mode effect added to standard video

I've previously said that Apple seems to have forgotten about Cinematic video mode. I said at the time that this was a real shame, because if Cinematic mode worked well, it would be a game-changer for treating the iPhone as a more serious video camera. So far, it hasn't come close to being satisfying.

But it looks like I was wrong: one of the new features of the iPhone 18 is that the Cinematic mode effect can now be applied to standard video as well.

It's certainly convenient not having to decide in advance whether to use this mode, but what interests me most is that Apple is paying attention to this feature again. This suggests Apple is indeed putting more resources into it, so we have reason to expect it will continue to improve, much like Portrait mode has. I'm very much looking forward to testing this feature.

Those are the features I think will have the biggest impact on me. What about you? If you've already upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, which features drove your decision? Feel free to share in the comments.
